issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette: Sam Rai, a 55‑year‑old Samoan man who has worked as a nanny for the past decade, returned to therapy after a long period of living in the shadow of a traumatic loss. He had been divorced for several years, and his daily routine involved caring for a group of school‑age children in a modest house on the outskirts of town. He was a steady presence for the parents, a reliable caretaker who had been hired because of his calm demeanor and the trust he had earned from families who valued his gentle touch and patience. The night that changed everything occurred when Sam’s younger brother, Tane, was caught in a sudden, violent altercation at a friends’ house. Sam was at a backyard barbecue, laughing and drinking with friends, when a group of strangers burst into the home, wielding knives and shouts. He saw Tane fall, the sharp glint of a blade catching the light on his wrist, the blood spattering a white shirt. He heard the scream of the victim’s mother, a sound that still echoes in his mind. The image of a single arm, twisted and bleeding, lodged itself in his consciousness. The scene was a sudden, brutal loss that left Sam’s mind flooded with terror, guilt, and the feeling that he had failed to intervene. In the days that followed, Sam found that any sight of a body part—a child's finger or a baby’s wrist—would snap him back to that night. The memories of the victim’s body, the smell of blood, and the echo of a scream haunted him, especially when the children he cared for talked about missing someone or when the parents spoke of death and funerals. These specific visual cues, reminders of the victim, and the theme of loss became daily triggers that pulled Sam into the night‑marish scene he had witnessed. Sam’s sense of self was shattered by the event. He believed he was weak, that he had been a powerless observer, and that he should have protected Tane. He felt as though he had been reduced to an object—an inert presence in a chaotic world. These negative appraisals seeped into the way he tried to reconstruct the night. When he attempted to explain what had happened to anyone, he lost the thread of the story; his narrative would halt at the moment he remembered the knife, and his mind would flicker to the sound of the scream. He could not piece the details together because the memory itself seemed fractured. The more he tried to describe the incident, the more he felt the weight of his perceived weakness, which in turn made the memory even more incomplete. The vivid, audible recollection of the screams in his head, the feeling of grief that washed over him when the memory resurfaced, all intensified his belief that he had failed. These feelings of failure made the triggers he encountered at work—seeing a child's hand, hearing a conversation about a loss—feel personally threatening, as if each reminder were a reminder of his own perceived inadequacy. The day to day at the daycare was not simply a matter of feeding and playing. The presence of children who were grieving, parents who spoke about death, and the small details that could trigger Sam’s intrusive images had a profound effect on his emotional stability. His negative appraisal of himself as weak and unprotective heightened his sensitivity to these cues. Whenever a child asked about a lost sibling or a parent mentioned a funeral, Sam felt his heart race, his chest tighten, and the memory of Tane’s twisted arm flood his mind. The triggers felt less like random accidents and more like personal assaults, reinforcing his belief that he was powerless. When he avoided a child's small hand that was too close for comfort or stayed away from a room where a parent was mourning, he reinforced the notion that he was acting like an object, detached and unresponsive. Each avoidance action deepened the cycle: his attempts to prevent discomfort only made him feel more disconnected and helpless, which in turn made the triggers even more potent. By the spring of the following year, Sam had begun to lose his role at the daycare. His avoidance of certain interactions and the tremors that would arise when he was near body parts or hearing about loss led to misunderstandings with the parents. They began to question his reliability, and he was eventually let go. The loss of his employment compounded his sense of failure and reinforced his belief that he could not protect those he cared for. The memories continued to replay, each recall reinforcing the negative appraisal that he was weak. He found himself withdrawing from social gatherings, avoiding conversations that could remind him of the event, and feeling a pervasive grief that seemed to cling to every day. When Sam finally decided to seek help, it was because the constant cycling of triggers, intrusive memories, and negative beliefs had begun to erode his sense of self and his ability to function. He was most afraid of reliving the night, fearing that each session would force him to relive the taste of blood and the scream. Yet he also held a fragile hope that understanding the connection between his self‑criticism and the haunting memories might release him from the cycle of pain and allow him to regain a sense of control and resilience in his work and personal life.
